title: Michael Flynn Jr. Amplifies Pizzagate While on Trump Transition Team
description_medium: In December 2016, Michael Flynn Jr., a member of Donald Trump’s transition team, repeated the false Pizzagate conspiracy theory about a Washington pizzeria. After a gunman entered Comet Ping Pong on December 4 to investigate the rumor, Flynn Jr. tweeted that it would remain a story until proven false. The episode involved Trump’s transition, but the documented posts were Flynn Jr.’s; they do not establish that Trump personally promoted the claim or refused a direct request to condemn it.
description_long: Pizzagate grew online in the weeks before the 2016 election from false claims that Hillary Clinton and campaign chairman John Podesta were connected to a child-trafficking ring at Comet Ping Pong, a Washington restaurant. The rumor spread after WikiLeaks released Podesta’s emails and users treated ordinary references to pizza as coded language. On December 4, 2016, a man entered the restaurant with a rifle, saying he wanted to investigate the rumor; he fired inside, and no one was injured. On December 5, Michael Flynn Jr., son of Trump’s incoming national security adviser and a member of the transition team, posted that Pizzagate would remain a story until proven false. The posts tied the false theory to people around the incoming administration and drew renewed attention because the conspiracy had prompted threats against the restaurant and its workers. Flynn Jr. was removed from the transition team the next day, according to contemporary reporting.

corrected_wording.prior_title: Trump Promotes 'Pizzagate' by Refusing to Condemn It (2016)
corrected_wording.reason: Contemporaneous accounts document Trump transition member Michael Flynn Jr. amplifying Pizzagate and his subsequent removal; they do not establish that Trump personally promoted the theory or refused a direct request to condemn it.

source_access_notes: PolitiFact’s contemporaneous reconstruction and Guardian reporting cover the same December 2016 posts and transition-team response.
rationale: The dated record identifies Michael Flynn Jr. as the person who posted about Pizzagate; the original title attributed an unverified act of refusal to Trump himself.

title: Trump Says Liz Cheney and Jan. 6 Committee Members Should Be Jailed (2024)
description_medium: In March 2024, Donald Trump posted that former Representative Liz Cheney “should go to jail” with the other members of the House committee that investigated January 6. His post followed a Republican-led report criticizing the earlier committee and its work with witness Cassidy Hutchinson. Cheney replied that Trump knew the evidence had long been available. The social-media statement was a call for jailing political opponents; it was not a criminal charge or court finding against Cheney.
description_long: On March 17, 2024, Donald Trump used Truth Social to say former Representative Liz Cheney should go to jail with the rest of the House committee that investigated the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. He reposted articles claiming that the bipartisan committee had suppressed evidence. The posts followed a Republican-led House report challenging part of Cassidy Hutchinson’s testimony about Trump’s actions on January 6. Cheney, the committee’s vice chair and its most prominent Republican member, replied that Trump and his lawyers had long had the evidence. At the time, neither Cheney nor the other committee members had been accused of a specific crime, ABC News reported. The panel’s final report had referred Trump to federal prosecutors for investigation over his conduct surrounding the attack. Trump also questioned whether Cassidy Hutchinson would be prosecuted over her testimony concerning his actions on January 6.

corrected_wording.prior_title: Trump Claims Liz Cheney Should Be Jailed for January 6 Committee Work (2023)
corrected_wording.reason: ABC News dates the post to March 2024 and reports Trump named Cheney and other committee members; the packet’s 2023 date is incorrect.

source_access_notes: ABC News directly reports the March 2024 Truth Social post, its context, and Cheney’s response.
rationale: Corrects the event year and identifies the statement as a social-media call for jail, distinct from an actual charge or finding.

title: Trump Calls for Pausing Ukraine Aid Until Biden-Family Investigations
description_medium: At a July 29, 2023, rally in Erie, Pennsylvania, Trump urged Congress to halt additional military aid to Ukraine until federal agencies provided evidence related to Republican investigations of Joe Biden and his family. He alleged that Ukraine had paid the family millions of dollars. The Associated Press reported that the claims centered on Hunter Biden’s payments from Burisma and that a Justice Department review had closed without sufficient evidence of wrongdoing. The rally remarks did not establish money laundering.
description_long: At a July 29, 2023, campaign rally in Erie, Pennsylvania, Donald Trump asked Republicans in Congress to withhold additional military support for Ukraine until the FBI, Justice Department, and IRS turned over evidence about the Biden family’s business dealings. Trump alleged that Ukraine had paid the family millions and linked that claim to U.S. support for Ukraine as it fought Russia’s invasion. The Associated Press reported that the allegations focused in part on payments Hunter Biden received from Burisma, a Ukrainian energy company. An FBI informant had made claims about payments to the Bidens, but a Justice Department review during Trump’s first term closed in 2020 with insufficient evidence of wrongdoing. The rally statement echoed Trump’s 2019 pressure on Ukraine to investigate the Bidens while U.S. military aid was at issue, which led to his first impeachment by the House and acquittal in the Senate. Trump’s 2023 demand was a political condition on future aid, not evidence that the family laundered money or that Ukraine had paid Joe Biden.

corrected_wording.prior_title: Trump Promotes Conspiracy That Ukraine War Is Biden-Family Money Laundering Scheme (2023)
corrected_wording.reason: The AP report covers Trump’s July 2023 demand to condition Ukraine aid on Biden investigations and his allegation of family payments; it does not establish a money-laundering scheme.

source_access_notes: The linked AP account is accessible and reports the rally, aid demand, allegation, and prior DOJ review.
rationale: Replaces an asserted money-laundering scheme with the source-backed rally demand and attributes the unproven payment allegation to Trump.

title: Trump Signs Revised Travel-Restriction Order 13780
description_medium: On March 6, 2017, Trump signed Executive Order 13780, a revised version of his January travel order. It suspended entry for 90 days for nationals of Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen, paused refugee admissions for 120 days, and capped fiscal-year refugee entries at 50,000. Iraq was removed from the country list, and the order included case-by-case waivers. Courts blocked key provisions before they took effect, prompting a Supreme Court dispute over the injunctions.
description_long: Executive Order 13780, signed March 6, 2017, replaced Trump’s January travel order after courts blocked parts of the earlier version. The revised order suspended entry for 90 days for nationals of six countries—Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen—removing Iraq from the list. It also paused refugee admissions for 120 days while agencies reviewed screening procedures, and capped refugee entries for fiscal year 2017 at 50,000. The order allowed case-by-case waivers. The administration said the measures were intended to review vetting and national-security procedures; challengers argued that the restrictions exceeded statutory authority and were motivated by anti-Muslim bias. Federal courts issued preliminary injunctions before the order’s March 16 effective date. In June, the Supreme Court partly stayed those injunctions, allowing restrictions for people without a credible claim of a bona fide relationship to a person or entity in the United States while preserving the injunctions for those with such ties. The order was a revised travel and refugee policy whose implementation was shaped by litigation, not a categorical prohibition on all Muslim travelers.

corrected_wording.reason: The entry is the March 2017 revised travel and refugee order; the replacement title names the order and avoids an editorial shorthand as the factual event title.

source_access_notes: The Supreme Court opinion and Federal Register text establish the order’s scope, effective date, and litigation posture.
rationale: Identifies the order’s limited country list, refugee provisions, exceptions, and court restrictions instead of treating it as an undifferentiated ban.

title: HHS Could Not Reach 1,475 Children After Sponsor Placement
description_medium: In April 2018, a Health and Human Services official told a Senate subcommittee that the agency had been unable to contact 1,475 migrant children after placing them with sponsors. HHS had called 7,635 sponsor households; it reached 6,075 children who were still living with their sponsors and recorded other outcomes for some of the rest. The number described failed follow-up contact, not proof that 1,475 children had disappeared or were trafficked.
description_long: The 1,475 figure came from a follow-up effort described by Health and Human Services in April 2018. HHS had placed unaccompanied migrant children with sponsors in communities around the country and later called 7,635 households to check on their status. Officials reported that 6,075 children were still living with their sponsors; 28 had run away, five had been deported, and 52 were living with someone else. Staff could not reach the remaining 1,475 children or their sponsors by phone. The testimony prompted questions from senators about HHS’s monitoring responsibilities after children left federal shelters and about safeguards intended to keep children safe. An inability to make contact was a serious oversight gap, but it did not establish that every child was missing from government records, had been abandoned, or had been trafficked. The follow-up gap became the focus of senators’ questions about the agency’s monitoring responsibilities after children left federal shelters.

corrected_wording.prior_title: Trump Administration Loses Track of 1,500 Migrant Children
corrected_wording.reason: HHS reported 1,475 children it could not reach through sponsor follow-up calls; that category does not establish that all were missing from federal custody or trafficked.

source_access_notes: Axios and PBS report the April 2018 Senate testimony and distinguish unable-to-contact cases from known outcomes.
rationale: Uses the reported follow-up totals to distinguish unsuccessful calls from known runaways, deportations, and children living elsewhere.

title: Trump Launches Immigration Crackdown with Day-One Orders
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Trump declared a national emergency at the southern border and signed orders that began a broad immigration-policy crackdown. He directed the Pentagon to support border-wall construction, detention space, and migrant transportation, and asked Defense to send troops if needed. The administration also ended the CBP One appointment program and moved to restrict asylum and birthright citizenship. These were day-one policy actions; they do not show that mass deportation raids occurred nationwide that day.
description_long: Within hours of taking office on January 20, 2025, President Trump declared illegal immigration a national emergency and issued a series of immigration directives. He ordered the Pentagon to provide support for border-wall construction, detention capacity, and migrant transportation, and authorized the defense secretary to send troops to the border as needed. The administration also ended the CBP One appointment system, canceling appointments that migrants had arranged to seek lawful entry. Other orders sought to restrict asylum and birthright citizenship, while Trump called for reinstating the “Remain in Mexico” program, which had required many non-Mexican asylum seekers to wait in Mexico for U.S. proceedings. The actions carried out his campaign promise to intensify border enforcement and expand deportations, but they were not the same as evidence that nationwide raids or mass removals had already begun on inauguration day. The scope of the day-one shift was visible in the emergency declaration, new agency instructions, military-support order, and immediate closure of a legal-entry pathway. Some measures, including the birthright-citizenship order, were challenged in court shortly after they were announced.

corrected_wording.prior_title: Mass Deportation Operations Begin on Day One of Second Term
corrected_wording.reason: Reuters documents day-one emergency and enforcement directives, but does not establish that nationwide mass deportation operations or city raids began that day.

source_access_notes: Reuters’ January 20 report documents the emergency declaration, military support direction, CBP One closure, and other initial measures.
rationale: Distinguishes the administration’s immediate policy and agency directives from later enforcement activity and avoids claiming nationwide raids began on day one.

title: Yosemite Ranger Shannon Joslin Fired After El Capitan Flag Display
description_medium: The National Park Service fired Yosemite ranger and wildlife biologist Shannon “SJ” Joslin after Joslin helped hang a 66-foot transgender Pride flag on El Capitan in May 2025. The flag flew for about two hours before the group removed it. Joslin said the display took place off duty and in a personal capacity. The NPS also said it was pursuing administrative action against several employees and possible criminal charges against some park visitors over demonstrations.
description_long: On May 20, 2025, a group of climbers hung a 66-foot transgender Pride flag from El Capitan in Yosemite National Park. The flag remained for about two hours before the group took it down. Shannon “SJ” Joslin, a Yosemite ranger and wildlife biologist who studied bats, said they helped organize and mount it while off duty, as a private citizen. Three months later, the National Park Service terminated Joslin, who had worked at the park for nearly five years. Joslin said the agency cited “failing to demonstrate acceptable conduct” and challenged the firing as a violation of their First Amendment rights. The NPS said it was pursuing administrative action against several park employees and possible criminal charges against some visitors accused of violating rules related to demonstrations. The next day, park management updated rules requiring permits for large banners in the wilderness and most demonstrations outside designated free-speech areas.

corrected_wording.prior_title: Federal Workers Fired for Being Transgender or Supporting Trans Rights
corrected_wording.reason: The accessible reporting supports the firing of one Yosemite employee, Shannon Joslin, after a specific flag display; it does not establish a government-wide pattern across agencies.

source_access_notes: AP reporting and CBS’s account with the NPS statement cover Joslin’s case and the related demonstration restrictions.
rationale: Narrows a government-wide firing claim to the documented Yosemite case and attributes the firing rationale and legal challenge to Joslin.
